lines.say: Here's a challenge. Make a qubit read one every time, without an X gate.
The trick is called interference, and noise cancelling headphones use it too.
They hear the noise around you, and play its mirror image.
Where the noise wave rises, theirs dips, so they cancel and the sound disappears.
Waves that rise and dip together get louder instead.
A qubit does this too. From zero, an H gate splits it into two paths, zero and one.
Each path carries an amplitude, a number that sets its chance and can be negative, drawn as an arrow.
A second H brings the paths together, and on each result, their arrows add.
On zero they point the same way and grow. On one, this H flips path one's arrow, so they cancel.
So H then H always reads zero.
Now add a Z gate in the middle. It shifts path one by half a wave, flipping its sign.
That's the headphone trick. Now the arrows cancel on zero, and add on one.
So H, Z, H reads one every time, no X gate needed.
Shift path one by a quarter wave instead, and you land halfway, at fifty fifty.
Unlike headphones, nothing is lost. The chance that vanishes from zero reappears on one.
And it isn't particles colliding. It's amplitudes, just numbers, adding to zero.
Probabilities alone could never cancel, because a chance is never negative.
Every quantum algorithm is a careful pattern of these cancellations.
Remember, amplitudes add like waves. In step they grow, and out of step they cancel.
